key_insight: Memory selection should reflect what each user is likely to need again, rather than follow one shared policy. The paper proposes using whether a fact is later retrieved and incorporated into a response as feedback for memory gating.
problem_solved: Language-model agents have limited memory capacity and cannot retain every fact. Shared memory policies overlook user-specific patterns of future reuse, potentially discarding useful information or keeping irrelevant details.
method: Study memory gating at the individual-fact level: deciding which extracted facts to retain.
Label facts based on whether they are later retrieved and incorporated into responses.
Target personalized gating using delayed, one-sided feedback; the provided abstract is truncated before the full formulation and evaluation.
impact: This approach could help practitioners use limited agent memory more effectively by prioritizing facts relevant to each user. Performance gains cannot be assessed from the provided excerpt.
visual_elements: Pipeline: conversation → extracted facts → memory gate → finite memory bank → future response.
Two user profiles highlighting different facts worth retaining.
Timeline connecting a stored fact to its later retrieval and use in a response.
Limited-capacity memory container showing retained versus discarded facts.
paper_title: Learning Personalized Memory Gating from Delayed One-Sided Feedback
paper_authors: Kaixuan Ji, Zixiang Chen, Wenting Zhao, Cheng Qian, Heng Wang
